reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Jackson went to the park with his dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Jackson wore his red cap. The cap was the color of a strawberry.

Then the trees began to move. "The wind came," said Dad. The wind blew a leaf right off a branch. The wind blew Jackson's cap off his head too. The cap flew over the grass. Jackson chased it. Dad caught it and put it back on. "The cap is light, so the wind took it," Jackson said.

Dad put Jackson's warm jacket on him. The jacket was heavy. The wind could not blow it away. Then gray clouds came. Rain fell. Dad opened the umbrella. "The rain can't get us," Jackson said. Dad smiled. "Here is our last stop," he said. They ran to the swings together.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Wren sat at the big table. She had a pencil and some paper. She wanted to write her name. Her name had four letters, W, R, E, N.

She held the pencil in her whole fist. She wrote a W. It came out wobbly. She wrote an R. That was wobbly too. The letters fell over like sleepy babies.

"Why do my letters fall over?" Wren asked.

"Look at your hand," said Grandma. Grandma sat close by her side. "Try pinching the pencil with two fingers."

Wren looked at her hand. She was squeezing with all five fingers. She let go. Then she pinched the pencil with her thumb and one finger. The pencil sat on her tall middle finger, like a little rest.

She wrote a W. It stood up straight. She wrote an R. It stood up too. "The pencil wobbles when I squeeze it all," Wren said. "It stands still when I pinch it."

"Yes," said Grandma. "Pinch, pinch, pinch."

Wren wrote an E. Wren wrote an N. There it was. W, R, E, N. Her name, all by itself on the paper. Her face felt warm and happy.

"I did it alone!" said Wren. She held the paper up high. "Look, Grandma, look at my name!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Jasmine skipped into the school cafeteria. It was her first day of school. She held her lunch box with two hands. Then she saw a big problem. All the seats were full!

"Where will I sit?" she asked. Then she looked again. One table had an empty spot. A boy sat there with his own lunch box. "Is this seat free?" she asked him. "Yes," he said. "My name is Ben."

Jasmine sat down next to Ben. She opened her lunch box. Mom had packed a tasty apple and a cheese sandwich. The kitchen at school made warm noodles too. Ben had noodles on his tray.

Jasmine took a big bite of her apple. Crunch! "Your apple is loud," Ben said with a giggle. Jasmine giggled too. "Apples go crunch because they are hard," she said. Ben bit his soft noodle. No crunch at all.

"We are lunch friends now," said Ben. Jasmine smiled big. First days are good with a friend. She skipped her feet under the table, tap tap tap.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Arthur ran up to Nia's door. He could not wait to play. Nia opened the door with a big smile.

"Come see my doll," she said. "She is sick today."

They went to the playroom. A doll lay in a small bed. Nia put a blanket on her. "She needs a doctor," Nia said.

Arthur looked around. He wanted to help. He found a blue coat in the toy box. He put it on. "I am the doctor now," he said. Nia found a little cup. "Here is her medicine," she said.

The doll would not drink. She was just plastic. Arthur held the cup near her mouth anyway. He made a little slurp sound. Nia clapped her hands. "She drank it! She feels better!"

"Why did the doll get better?" Arthur asked. He thought hard. "Because we pretended the medicine worked," he said. Nia nodded fast.

"Now she needs a nap," Nia said. They made a nest of soft pillows. They tucked the doll in. Arthur whispered, "Sleep tight, little baby."

The doll's eyes stayed open. That was okay. In the game, her eyes were closed.

Then Nia said, "The baby is hungry when she wakes up." Arthur grinned. "I will make soup!" He stirred a pretend pot with a big spoon.

The doorbell rang. It was Arthur's dad. "One more minute," Arthur called. He fed the doll one last spoonful. "All done," he said. "She is a healthy baby now."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Muhammad sat at the dinner table. His eyes felt heavy. His spoon went down, down to his plate. He did not eat his rice.

"Papa, my eyes want to close," he said. Papa looked at him. "You did not nap today," said Papa. Muhammad thought about that. No nap. Now sleepy. "No nap makes me sleepy," he said.

Mama filled his cup with milk. He drank it all. Then he ate three small bites of rice. His tummy felt warm.

After dinner, Mama ran the bath. The water was warm and bubbly. Muhammad washed his toes and his arms. Then he put on his soft blue pajamas. He buttoned the top button all by himself.

Papa carried him past the desk by the window. The window was open a little. A cool breeze came in. Muhammad yawned a big yawn.

"Sleep now," Papa said. Muhammad closed his eyes. The breeze touched his cheek, soft and slow.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Maya was four today. Her party was at the big park. Grandma set the cake on the table. Mom put four candles on top. Maya wanted to blow them out.

Maya lit the candles with Dad's help. Then the wind blew. One candle went out. Then another went out. Maya frowned. "Why do they go out?" she asked. "The wind is blowing them," said Dad. Maya held her hands around the candles. The wind could not get in. The candles stayed lit.

"Quick, sing to me!" said Maya. Everyone sang the birthday song. When the song was done, Maya took a big breath. She blew and blew. All four candles went out at once. Everyone clapped.

Then Maya grabbed her juice cup to cheer. She waved it too fast. The juice began to spill. Grandma caught it with a napkin. "Easy," said Grandma, and she hugged her. At the next table, Ben sat very still and looked green from spinning on the merry-go-round. "Are you sick?" Maya asked. "A little," said Ben. So he sat by Grandma too, and they shared the cake.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Hazel went to the store with Dad. She held her bunny in her hand. Then she saw the apples. She let go of bunny to pick one up. When Dad said "Let's go," Hazel looked down. Bunny was gone.

Hazel walked back to the apples. No bunny there. She felt sad and slow in her feet. Then she thought about what she did. She had picked up an apple first. So bunny must have fallen near the apples. She looked under the apple shelf. She saw something soft and white. It was bunny! "You fell down because I let go," Hazel said. She gave bunny a big hug.

Dad put the apples in the cart. He gave Hazel a juice box, too. It had a picture of a blue lake on it. "Make bunny a seat," Dad said. So Hazel made a seat with her coat. Bunny sat in the cart all the way home. Hazel held the juice box and smiled at the little lake. "We found you," she whispered to bunny.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Athena went to the backyard with Dad. She wanted to find her red ball. "Stay close to me," said Dad. Athena stayed close to Dad.

She heard a loud train far away. Choo, choo! The train was far, far away. That was neat. Athena did not go near the train. Trains are big and fast. She just listened with Dad.

Then she saw the red ball. It sat by the grill. The grill was hot. Athena could feel the warm air on her face. She stopped her feet. "Hot," she said. She did not touch the grill. She put her hands behind her back, like Dad taught her. Hot things can hurt you.

Dad turned the grill off. They waited. Athena began to count. "One, two, three, four, five." She touched the air above the grill. Now the air was cool. The grill was cold now. Cold things are safe to touch.

Athena picked up her ball. "The grill got cold because you turned it off," she said. Dad smiled. "That's right. You waited, and you stayed close." Athena hugged her red ball. She rolled it on the grass, back and forth. "Safe and sound," said Dad. Athena rolled the ball again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Ellie sat on the big doctor bed. Rain went tap, tap, tap on the window. The nurse came in with a tiny silver tray. "One, two, three," said the nurse. "On three, blow out like birthday candles." Ellie held Mama's hand. She squeezed it. Squeeze, one, two, three. Ellie took a big breath and blew. She blew and blew, like blowing out candles on a cake. "All done!" said the nurse. Ellie looked at her arm. There was a small round bandage on it. "It was just a tiny pinch," said Ellie. "It went away fast because I blew it out." "What a smart girl," said Mama.

Afterward they went to the ice cream shop. The rain had stopped. The sun was warm, warm like fire. Ellie got pink strawberry ice cream. One lick, two licks, three. "My favorite," she said, and she held up her bandage for the scoop of strawberry to see.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Ayla was at Grandma's house. It was a cloudy day. "We can play inside," said Grandma.

Grandma had a big box of letters. Each letter was a little wooden shape. Ayla tipped them out on the rug in the room. They made a clicky sound on the floor.

Ayla picked up a curvy letter. It looked like a snake. "S," said Grandma. "It says sss." Ayla slid the letter on the rug. "Sss," she said, like a snake hissing.

Then she held up a round letter. "Is this S too?" she asked. Grandma shook her head. "That is O. It says ohh." Ayla turned it around and around. The O looked the same every way she turned it! But when she turned the S, it looked different. It fell over and lay like a sleepy snake.

"Oh," said Ayla. "The S is wiggly. The O is round." She put S on the rug. She put O next to it. "Sss, ohh," she said.

"Shall we find your letter?" asked Grandma. "A for Ayla. It says ahh." Ayla dug in the pile. Click, click went the letters. Then she found one with two pointy legs. She held it up high.

"Ahh!" she called out. Grandma clapped. Ayla hugged the letter to her chest.

"Ah," she whispered to it, "you are mine."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Nathan walked up the big hill with his dad. It was Diwali night. Lots of little lamps glowed in the dark. They smelled like smoke and sweet flowers.

Nathan held his own clay lamp. He wanted to light it. He touched his wick to Dad's flame. It did not light. He tried again. Still dark. "Tell me why, Dad," Nathan said. Dad just smiled. "Try one more time. Wait a little first."

Nathan looked at his lamp. He remembered. He had washed his hands before dinner. Water had dripped on the wick. The wick was wet. So Nathan waited. He held the lamp in the warm air. He watched other lamps twinkle on the hill. He waited some more.

Then he touched his wick to Dad's flame again. This time it lit! A tiny orange light popped up. "The wick was wet," Nathan said. "Wet wicks do not light. Now it is dry!" Dad clapped. Nathan set his lamp on the grass. It glowed beside all the others.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Lea stood by the school gate. She held her small toy rabbit tight. "What if the teacher does not know my name?" she asked. Mama knelt down next to her. "Let's go and see," said Mama.

A teacher smiled at the gate. Lea hid behind Mama's legs. Then the teacher said, "Hello, Lea!" Lea looked up. How did the teacher know? She looked down at her shirt. A red tag was pinned there. It had her name on it. Letters make the tag say a name, she thought. The teacher read the tag, so the teacher knew her.

Lea let go of Mama's hand. She ran to the high slide. "Come play, rabbit," she said. She gave her animal a big hug at the top. "The teacher knows me," said Lea. "My tag said so."

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Luna ran up to the bookmobile. It was a little truck full of books. Luna wanted a book about bunnies. She found one with a soft white bunny on the cover.

A kind man gave Luna her very first library card. "Mine!" said Luna. She held it tight. Then she asked, "Can I keep the bunny book forever?" The man shook his head. "You borrow it," he said. "You take it home. Then you bring it back. Other kids want to read it too." Luna looked at the book. She moved it close to her chest. "Bring it back," she said. "So Sam can read it too. Sam likes bunnies." The man smiled. "Yes. That is how it works."

Luna gave the man her card. He stamped the book. Luna held the book like a gift. She would read it at home, in her cozy bed. When the bookmobile came back, her bag would be empty, and she would give the bunny book back. Then she would get a new one. "Bye, truck!" said Luna. She waved and waved.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Jasmine stood in the backyard with a red beanbag. Her dog, Biscuit, sat by her feet. He was big and furry. Dad held up a hoop. "Try again," he said.

Jasmine threw the beanbag. It went too low. It hit the grass. Biscuit ran to it and gave it a lick. "No, Biscuit," said Jasmine. She laughed and took it back. She looked at the hoop. It was up high. She looked at her hands. She held the beanbag way down by her knees. That was why it went too low.

So she lifted her hands up high. "One, two, three, throw!" she said. The beanbag flew up and went right in. Dad clapped. Biscuit barked.

Then Dad rolled her a big blue ball. Jasmine held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. It rolled under the bush. She got it and tried again. This time she held out both hands. She pulled them in close to her tummy. The big ball landed right in her arms. "I caught it!" she said. Biscuit jumped up and licked her cheek. Jasmine patted his furry head. "One, two, three, throw!" she said, and threw the ball to Dad.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Emile sat in the vet's office with a small box. Inside the box was a gray kitten. The kitten was going home with him today. Emile wanted to hold her right away.

The vet smiled. "New cats need a quiet house," she said. "Loud noise makes them hide."

At home, Emile clapped his hands. "Come out, kitty!" he called. The kitten ran under the couch. Emile could not see her at all. It was getting late, almost bedtime.

Then Emile remembered. Loud noise makes them hide. So he sat down very still. He whispered, "Kitty, kitty." He tapped one finger on the floor, soft, soft.

A small gray nose peeked out. Then the whole kitten came out. She walked to Emile and rubbed his leg.

Emile gave her a gentle kiss on her head. "I love you, kitty," he whispered.

The kitten curled up in his lap and went to sleep.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Clara sat at the big art table. She was painting a butterfly. It had red wings and yellow dots. "So cute," she said. She fished in the crayon box for a black one. She wanted to add little legs.

Clara pressed her finger on the wing. The paint smeared. Now there was a red spot on her finger and a big smudge on the wing. "Oh no," said Clara. She looked at her finger. She looked at the wing. Why did it smear?

She touched the yellow dots next. Those were dry. Nothing came off. "The wet paint smears," said Clara. "The dry paint stays." So she waited. She counted to ten, twice. Then she touched the wing again. It felt dry and smooth. The paint stayed on the paper, right where she put it.

Clara picked up the black crayon. She drew the little legs. The butterfly was done. "Look at you," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay at Maeva's house for a whole week. Maeva wanted to take him to the park. But first Grandpa said, "I need my nap." After lunch he slept in the big chair.

Maeva could not wait. She wanted to show him the slide. So she called to him from the door. "The park is far, Grandpa! Get up!" She did not mean to yell, but she did. Grandpa woke up fast. He sat up and rubbed his eyes. He looked tired still.

Mom gave Maeva a small job. "Make him a snack for the walk," she said. Maeva put bread and cheese in a little bag. She waited by the door, very quiet. She hummed a tiny song instead of calling.

Soon Grandpa came out in his blue coat. "My nap is done," he said, smiling. Maeva held his hand. They walked to the park together. Grandpa went down the slide, once, very slowly. Then something fell out of his pocket. It was a red balloon! "For you," said Grandpa. The balloon bobbed up in the sun. Maeva jumped for it and held the string tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Paisley wanted to help at snack time. Miss Dana held up the tray. "Can you count out crackers for your table?" she asked. Paisley nodded big.

She sang the counting song in her head. "One, two, three, four, five." She put five crackers in a bowl. Then she tried to go on. "Seven, nine, ten!" she sang out loud.

Ben started to giggle. "That is a joke song," he said. "You skipped some!"

Paisley looked at her bowl. It did not look full enough. She counted the children at the table. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. Eight friends, and only five crackers.

She closed her eyes. She sang the song slowly, like Miss Dana sang it. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." She touched a cracker on each word. Now the bowl was full.

"Now everyone gets one," said Ben. He took his cracker and smiled.

Paisley could see her bowl. Eight crackers, eight friends. "The song has to go in order," she told Ben. "If you skip, the crackers skip too."

Then Miss Maya tapped her sharp pencil on the table. "Ten napkins next, Paisley."

"One, two, three, four," sang Paisley.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Julia put on her pajama shirt. It was soft and blue. But her teddy bear was gone.

Julia looked under the bed. It was dark there. Her tummy felt tight. "I am scared," she said. She grabbed her flashlight. The light made the dark go away. The tight tummy went away too.

Then she heard a bump. Julia got angry. She stomped her foot. "Who took my bear?" she said. She peeked in the toy box. There was teddy, stuck under a big book!

Julia pulled him out. "You hid from me!" she said. She felt so happy she did a little dance. Then Mama came in. "Time for bed," said Mama. Julia felt excited. She hugged teddy tight.

"Teddy was sad under the book," Julia said. "Now he is not sad." She gave him a sweet kiss on his nose. She pulled the blanket up. The flashlight clicked off. "Night night, teddy," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Jack had a new pet. It was a shiny gold fish. The fish swam in a little bowl. Jack held his dad's hand all the way home.

"I will feed him now," said Jack. He got a big spoon. He put in a big spoon of food. The bowl got cloudy. The food made the water yucky. The fish hid behind a little green plant.

"That is too much food," said Dad. Dad helped pour out the old water. He added clean water. "Just a tiny pinch," said Dad. Jack took a tiny pinch. He dropped it in. The water stayed clear. The fish came out and ate it up.

"Too much food made the water bad," said Jack. "A tiny pinch is just right." The fish swam in circles. The birds began to sing outside the window. Dad put his arm around Jack. The fish blew a little bubble. "Good night, fish," said Jack.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Jacob went to the backyard with Grandpa. The sun was hot on the grass. Jacob wanted to play with the grill. It was black and big. "Not that," said Grandpa. "Hot things can hurt you." Grandpa put his hand far from the grill. He let Jacob feel the warm air. "See? Hot," said Grandpa. Jacob felt the hot air on his little hand. He pulled his hand back fast.

Then Jacob saw a brown stone in the grass. He touched the stone. It was not hot. It was cold and smooth. "This one is cold," Jacob said. Grandpa smiled. "Yes. Cold stones are safe to hold."

Jacob put the stone in his pocket. He wanted to show it to Mama. "Stay close to me," said Grandpa. Jacob stayed close. He held Grandpa's hand. They walked to the porch together. Jacob showed Mama the cold brown stone. "Cold stone," said Jacob. Mama said, "What a good finder you are." Jacob sat down by Grandpa and held his stone.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Charles sat at the dinner table. His hands still had blue paint on them from painting a dog. Mom said, "Wash first, then eat." That was a table rule.

The bread basket came around. Charles wanted two rolls. Dad said, "One for now. Then the basket goes around." Charles took one roll. He passed the basket to his sister. She was asleep in her chair, so he passed it on to Mom.

Then the mashed potatoes came. Charles reached for the big spoon. His cousin Leo reached too. Their hands bumped. "Who goes first?" Charles asked. Mom said, "You went first last night. Tonight Leo goes first." So Charles waited. Leo took some, then Charles took some. Then Leo passed him the butter without being asked.

Charles took a bite of his roll. It was warm and soft. "Sharing goes around, and around, and around," he said. Everyone began to laugh. Even the baby woke up and laughed too. Charles gave her a little wave, and she waved back with her tiny paint-free hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Brooks put on his swim cap. It had white sheep on it. His sheep cap was easy to see. His towel was snowy white and soft.

Today was the swim meet. It was the last one of the season. Brooks swam on the Turtles. He waited at the edge for his turn. Lily swam first. Then Ben. Then it was Brooks. He jumped in and kicked hard. He touched the wall. Maya went next. She tagged Maya's hand first. Then Maya could go. One swimmer, then the next.

Brooks looked for his goggles. Where did they go? He peeked under the towel. They did not hide there. He peeked in his bag. There they were. "I found them," said Brooks. Coach gave him a green ribbon. It was for the whole season. Brooks held it up high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story: Aiden sat at the big table in the hall. Grandma held out her hand. "We say our blessing first," she said. Aiden picked up his cookie instead. He took a big bite. "Too late!" said Grandma. She laughed. "We need to say it before we eat." Aiden looked at his cookie. Half of it was gone already. "Oh no," he said. He put the cookie down. He put his hands together, just like Grandma. He closed his eyes tight. His boot tapped the floor under the table. "Thank you for the food," he said. "That is true," said Grandma. "Now we eat!" Aiden picked up his cookie again. Next time, he said the blessing first. Then he took the very first bite. "Before, not after!" said Aiden. Grandma clapped her hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Kayden wanted a warm cookie. He could not find one. "Where are the cookies?" he asked.

First he used his eyes. He saw the tall counter. He saw a big bowl. No cookies yet. Then he used his ears. He heard a beep, beep. The oven was hot! It was winter, so the warm oven felt nice on his face.

Next he used his nose. He sniffed, sniff, sniff. He smelled something sweet. His nose knew that smell! He remembered it from Grandma's house. He followed the sweet smell right to the oven.

Ding! The cookies were done. Mom gave him one. He touched it with his fingers. Warm! He took a little bite. His tongue tasted sugar and chocolate. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three cookies!"

"The oven beeped, so the cookies were done," Kayden said. "And my smelly socks did not help at all. Only my nose helped!"

Mom laughed. "That's right, sweet boy."

Kayden took another warm, sweet bite.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Blake wanted juice at daycare. The juice was hot from the sun. "Too hot," she said.

Miss Kim showed her a big pitcher. "The big pitcher is cold from the fridge." Blake touched it. Cold! She poured a little hot juice and a little cold juice. She sipped it. Warm. Just right.

Then Blake heard a boy talk about his slow snail. It moved so slow. Blake ran fast to see. "Wow, you are fast," said the boy. "My snail is small and slow. You are big and fast." Blake sat down alone next to the snail. She waited. The snail climbed up. Its bottom slid along the leaf. It went so slow, but it did not stop. "Look, it got to the top!" said Blake. "Slow can do it too."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Theodore went to the library with his mama. He wanted a book about a spider. "Here is one," said Mama. The cover had a black spider on a web. Theodore held it tight. "I want to keep it forever," he said. He opened the front cover first. He turned page one, then page two, then page three. The pages went front to back. The words on the page told the spider story. "The words talk to me," said Theodore.

Mama smiled softly. She showed him a little card. "The book has to come back on this day," she said. "Other kids want to read it too." Theodore hugged the spider book. "One book about a spider. One book about how to bake bread. One book about a bear asleep in winter." He counted his three books. At home, he read the spider book two times. Then he put it by the door. "I will bring you back," he whispered to the spider, "so a friend can read you too."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Clara ran to school with a purple backpack. Inside was a horse magnet for show and tell. She was so excited. Show and tell was her favorite thing.

But at school, her friend Ben sat alone. His face looked sad. His bunny toy was lost. Then Max grabbed Ben's crayons, and Ben got angry. His face turned red.

Then thunder boomed outside. A big boom! Clara felt scared. She held her magnet tight.

Then she had an idea. "Ben, let's look for bunny," she said. They looked under the table. They looked in the box. The magnet pulled the table clip, cling! And there was bunny, stuck to a chair leg.

"I found him!" said Ben. A big smile filled his face.

"You were sad," said Clara. "Now you are happy."

Thunder boomed again. But now they laughed together. Even the scary boom felt small.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Sofia stood in the school hallway. Her red backpack was heavy on her back. The hallway had many little doors and many hooks on the wall. So many hooks! Which one was hers?

Sofa looked up at the hooks. Each hook had a little card on it. The cards had names on them. She could not read big words yet. But she knew her own name. It started with an S. She walked slowly and looked at each card.

Then she saw it. A card with Sofia on it. The card was red, just like her backpack. She hung her backpack on that hook. It fit! Why did that hook hold her backpack? Because the hook had her name on it. "The name tells me where to go," she said. She said it out loud, soft and slow.

A boy came to stand beside her. He looked sad and a bit mixed up. He could not find his name. Sofia pointed at the cards. "Look for the one with your name," she said. He found a card with a sheep drawn on it, and his name under the sheep. He hung up his bag too. Then he smiled at Sofia.

The teacher opened the big door. "Come in, friends," she said. Sofia took one more look at her red card. Then she walked in.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
John sat in his car seat. He was hungry. "My snack, please," he said. Mom handed him a warm bottle of juice. The sun shone on it through the window. The juice got hot. John made a sad face. Mom put the bottle in the cool shade behind her seat. Soon the juice was cold again. John drank it all up.

A big truck sat next to them. It went very slow. A small car zoomed by. It went fast. John pointed at the truck. "Big is slow," he said. "Small is fast."

Then a big dog in the small car barked at them. It had a clean white bone in its mouth. John waved at the dog. The dog wagged its tail.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Maya ran into the garage. Dad kept his old drum kit there. Today it was hers to try!

She picked up a drumstick. She hit the drum very hard. BOOM! The drumstick bounced right out of her hand. It flew onto Dad's work bag.

"Oh no!" said Maya. She got the stick back.

Maya tried again. This time she held the stick with a loose hand. She tapped the drum. Boom, boom, boom. The stick stayed right in her grip!

"You did it!" said Dad. "Keep tapping, Maya!"

Maya tapped faster. Boom boom boom! She smiled big.

"When I squeeze too hard, the stick jumps away," Maya said. "When my hand is soft, the stick stays!"

She tapped and tapped. Boom boom boom, all the way to lunch time.

"Can we play again after my nap?" she asked.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Zayn put on his red shirt. His team was called the Red Foxes. They played inside the big room at the community center. The floor was cold under his feet, so he jumped up and down.

"Kick, kick, pass," said Coach Kim. Zayn ran to the ball. He kicked it too hard. The ball went far, far away. Then he saw why. A big kick makes the ball go far. A little kick makes it go close. He tried a little kick. One, two, three, tap. The ball rolled right to his friend Mia.

Mia caught it with her feet. She did not fall. She waved at Zayn. "Nice pass!" she said. Zayn jumped high. He was a Red Fox who could pass.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
William was on the swim team. Every Saturday morning the pool was full of kids. The coach gave William a small red kickboard. "Hold it tight," said the coach. "Kick to the other side."

William held the board and kicked. But his kicks were tiny, like a little fish. He stayed in one spot. The water was cool on his toes. A big kid zoomed past him with big, slow kicks. William looked and looked.

Then William tried big, slow kicks too. Whoosh! The water pushed him along. He was moving! He went all the way to the wall. "My big kicks made me go fast," said William.

A small girl next to him was stuck like he had been. Her feet wiggled but she did not move. William paddled over to her. "Kick big and slow," he said. "Watch me." She watched. Then she kicked big and slow. Whoosh! She moved too.

"Fast legs, slow legs, fast legs!" she laughed. At the end, the coach gave them both a ribbon. William held his up high. "I got this because I kicked big," he said. The small girl splashed him with a happy kick.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Lily ran to the reading corner. She saw the librarian, Miss Jo, holding something small.

"This is for you," said Miss Jo. "Your very own library card."

Lily held it up high. The card had a red bird on it. "Now I can take a book home!" said Lily. "A real book, at my house!"

She picked a big book about a fire truck. The truck was red like a ball of fire. The cover felt rough on her hands. Miss Jo put the card on a string so it could hang around Lily's neck.

"I will keep this book forever and ever," said Lily. She hugged it tight.

Miss Jo smiled. "Let's try it first," she said. "Stamp, stamp." She put a date in the book.

At home, Lily read the book ten times. Then Sam came over. Sam wanted the fire truck book too.

"But it is mine," said Lily.

"It was mine first," said Sam. "I read it at the library. Now it is your turn. Then it is my turn again."

Lily looked at the date in the book. The book had to go back so Sam could read it. "The book comes back because other kids want it," said Lily.

She ran back to the library with Miss Jo. Then she got a new book about a yellow duck. Sam waved the fire truck book at her.

"Your turn again soon," said Sam.

"Next time I get two books," said Lily.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Ethan wants the red crayon at school. Mia has it. She is drawing a big dragon.

Ethan grabs the crayon. Mia begins to cry. The dragon loses one wing.

"Sorry, Mia," Ethan says. He gives the crayon back. Mia adds two more wings. Now the dragon can fly in the pretend clouds.

"Can I help you color, please?" Ethan asks. Mia nods. She hands him a blue crayon. It feels like a magic wand.

Ethan draws gentle rain. "The dragon needs rain to grow," he says. Mia laughs.

At clean-up time, Ethan drops the crayon box. All the colors roll under the table. "Can you help me, Teacher?" he asks. The teacher smiles and reaches down.

"I said help, so you helped me," Ethan says. "The crayons come out because we both reached!"

"You're welcome," says the teacher. "And thank you for asking so nicely."

Ethan holds up the blue crayon like a sword. "The magic wand works best with please," he whispers to the dragon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
The car was going fast. William sat in his big seat. He wanted to draw a dog. He looked in his bag for his red crayon.

But the red crayon was missing! William looked and looked. He found a dinosaur. That was a toy, not a crayon. He found an apple. That was food, not a crayon. He found a cracker, too. Yum. He took a big bite.

Then Mom turned the car. The bag tipped over. Everything slid to one side. "The car turned, so my things slid," said William. And there, under the apple, was the red crayon! It had been hiding all along.

William reached for it. He got it! He held it up high. "I found it!" he said. Mom smiled. William drew a big red dog on his paper. The dog had a long tail. "Next I will draw the apple," said William. He took another happy bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Michael sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to make a paper fish. Grandma gave him paper, glue, and shiny dots.

Michael put the shiny dots on the paper. He picked up the paper to show Grandma. The dots fell off. They rolled onto the floor. Michael felt sad. "My dots fell down," he said.

Grandma smiled softly. She put glue on the paper. The glue felt cold and slimy on Michael's fingers. Michael put a dot on the glue. He lifted the paper up high. The dot stayed on. It did not fall.

"The glue holds it!" said Michael. He put glue on the tail too. He put more dots on the fish. Then he held it up for Grandma to see. "Look, Grandma. My fish has shiny spots now."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Madelyn wanted a letter from Grandma. Yesterday, Mom put a letter in the mailbox. Madelyn saw Mom drop it in. The little door clanked shut. "It went away," said Madelyn. "The mail truck takes it," said Mom.

Today, Madelyn ran to the mailbox. She pulled hard. The door was stuck. She wiggled it. Then it opened. The mailbox was empty. "Where is Grandma's letter?" she asked. "It is still going," said Mom. "The truck is driving now. Grandma gets it later."

Madelyn frowned. "Later is a long time," she said. Mom smiled. "Not so long. Today the letter rides in the truck. Tomorrow it gets to Grandma." Madelyn looked at the road. The sun was warm on the mailbox. "Then Grandma reads it tomorrow," she said.

"Then she writes back," said Mom. Madelyn clapped her hands. "Her letter comes next!" she said. She patted the mailbox. "Goodbye, little box. I will see you tomorrow." Then she ran inside to draw a picture for Grandma.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Hailey wanted the red truck. Her brother Ben had the red truck. He pushed it on the floor. It went fast.

"Give it to me," Hailey said. Ben held it tight. His face looked sad. Hailey grabbed, and Ben cried. Then Mama came. She held up a little timer. "You can take turns," she said. "Ben goes first." The timer ticked. Hailey waited. Then it rang, ding! Ben gave her the truck. Now Hailey pushed it fast on the floor. When the timer rang again, she gave it back.

Hailey smiled. "The timer helps us share," she said. Ben smiled too. They sat close together. The truck rolled past them both. "It goes to me, then to you," said Hailey. Outside, a car went down the street. "Just like that car," said Ben. "One at a time."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Carter wants to find the top of the big slide. But his shoes are dirty. Ms. Amy says, "Wipe them first." Carter waits. He wipes and wipes. Now his shoes are clean.

He climbs up. A big boy runs fast past him. Carter goes slow. Slow feet do not slip. He hears the big boy say, "Ouch!" The big boy went too fast and fell down on his bottom.

Carter keeps going slow, step by step. He gets to the top. He sits down. He puts his hands up. He slides down fast. The wind feels cold on his face. At the bottom, his cheeks feel hot. He laughs and says, "Big slide, fast slide!"

Ms. Amy claps. "Slow up, fast down," she says. Carter nods. He runs to the back of the line. He wants to go again.
